Package org.jdesktop.lg3d.mandela.api

Class MandelaScriptEngine

java.lang.Object
javax.script.AbstractScriptEngine
org.jdesktop.lg3d.mandela.api.MandelaScriptEngine
All Implemented Interfaces:
Compilable, Invocable, ScriptEngine
public final class MandelaScriptEngine extends AbstractScriptEngine implements Compilable, Invocable
Mandela as a javax.script engine, so a host that already embeds one script engine gets a second without learning a new API.

The class is a translation layer, not a second implementation: one Runtime does the parsing, compiling and running, and everything here converts the JSR-223 shapes — Bindings, ScriptContext, ScriptException — into the Mandela shapes they correspond to. Two engines would drift, and the desktop's own hosts (Espresso, the Web Browser) drive a Runtime directly, so what a third-party integration sees through JSR-223 is exactly what the desktop runs.

What one eval does

  1. announces the engine's own attributes into the engine scope, as every compliant engine does;
  2. pushes the engine and global Bindings into the runtime's globals, each converted with Interop.toMandela(java.lang.Object);
  3. re-points the console at ScriptContext.getWriter() and ScriptContext.getErrorWriter(), so println lands where the host asked for it;
  4. compiles, then runs: a LangException or MandelaError becomes a ScriptException carrying the real file, line and column, which is what lets an IDE gutter show it;
  5. writes back into the engine scope, in plain Java form, every name the run created, replaced or received as a binding, and returns the program's last value through Interop.toJava(java.lang.Object).

What a binding cannot be

A binding with no Mandela form — an arbitrary POJO, which Interop refuses on purpose — stays on the host's side of the window: engine.get(key) still returns it and the script sees an undefined name. Skipping it quietly beats throwing at the boundary for a value the script never mentions, and beats reflecting on it, which is how a sandbox gets bypassed.

Sandbox and threads

The default engine is Capabilities.console(): a console, no files, no environment, no network, no threads, no JVM. A host that means more passes its own Capabilities, or the Runtime it already configured, to the constructor. Every entry point synchronizes on the engine, which is the single-threaded serial model JSR-223 assumes; a host that wants concurrency builds one engine per thread, which is cheap.

Use


 ScriptEngine engine = new ScriptEngineManager().getEngineByName("mandela");
 engine.put("prices", List.of(12.5, 40.0));
 engine.put("rate", 0.05);
 Object total = engine.eval("""
         let tax = { v -> v * rate }
         prices.map(tax).sum()
         """);
 // total is a Double, and ((Invocable) engine).invokeFunction("tax", 9.0) works

    • MandelaScriptEngine

      public MandelaScriptEngine(ScriptEngineFactory factory, Runtime runtime)
      Wraps an engine the host already configured.

      This is the constructor Espresso and the Web Browser use: they hold a Runtime with their own capabilities, console and host functions, and they add the JSR-223 door to it rather than build a second engine that would keep a separate set of names from the one their panels show.

      Parameters:
      factory - the factory that asked for this engine
      runtime - the engine to drive, reused as-is

    • knownGlobals

      public Set<String> knownGlobals()
      The names a program on this engine may read without declaring them: the library's globals plus every binding and host function pushed so far.

      An editor reads this for completion. It is why binding a host function before compiling matters — a name the compiler knows is a name the editor can offer.

      Returns:
      a snapshot of the visible names
